01.actor: The Sages in Rabbi's days; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
01.event: The Sages sought to permit the Gibeonites
01.turn: Rabbi objects that the altar's share cannot be permitted
01.outcome: Implied that the proposal was not adopted
01.summary: In Rabbi's days the Sages wanted to permit the Gibeonites to marry into the community. Rabbi answered that even if they could waive their own share, no one could waive the altar's share.
01.missing: Any action beyond the proposal and the reply; the outcome is only implied
01.reason: Seeking to permit and replying are legislative speech acts. There is no event beyond speaking, and the disagreement is ordinary legal debate, so it is not a story.

02.event: A bill of divorce lay nearer to her than to her husband and was lost; her husband later died
02.turn: The court doubted whether the divorce had taken effect
02.outcome: They required her to undergo halitza
02.summary: Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi of an incident in which a bill of divorce was closer to the woman than to the husband. When the husband died, they required her to perform halitza.
02.missing: The incident itself is only named. Its details come from the legal context and the translator's gloss
02.reason: A case is only alluded to and then ruled on. Nothing else is narrated besides the ruling, so under R-C0 (2026-10-25) it is not a story.

03.missing: Any one-time event. The passage holds Rabbi Yohanan's recollections of his time studying and the Gemara's reconciliation of his statements
03.reason: These are reports of a study period and of crowded seating, cited as teaching. Nothing happens and nothing changes.

04.actor: Rav Nahman; a woman from Mehoza married to a man of Neharde'a
04.event: The couple come before Rav Nahman, and he recognizes from her accent that she is from Mehoza
04.turn: He rules by Babylonia's custom (Rav). They point out that she is marrying into Neharde'a
04.outcome: Rav Nahman reverses himself and applies Neharde'a's custom (Shmuel)
04.summary: A woman from Mehoza married to a man from Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman. He heard from her accent where she came from and ruled by Rav's custom. When they objected that she was marrying into Neharde'a, he changed his ruling to Shmuel's custom.
04.reason: There is a case before a rabbi with a perception (the accent) and a reversal of the ruling, which gives some change beyond a single ruling. It is still mostly speech, so borderline.

05.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, and Hasa died without leaving instructions
05.turn: The claimants came before Rav Nahman
05.outcome: Rav Nahman awarded the goblet to the depositor because Hasa was not wealthy and the depositor gave a distinguishing mark
05.summary: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without saying anything about it. When they came before Rav Nahman, he ruled for the depositor: Hasa was known not to be wealthy, and the man could identify the goblet.
05.reason: Two narrated events (the deposit and the death) are followed by a ruling, the shape of the cow case. But the resolution is a ruling and the passage ends in legal qualification, so borderline.

06.event: A man prepared a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after the death of the woman's husband
06.outcome: Rava made him forfeit his feast
06.summary: A man prepared a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after the woman was widowed, and Rava made him forfeit the feast. The Gemara then explains that it was really a wedding feast.
06.missing: The incident is cited briefly as evidence inside a legal discussion
06.reason: An incident is alluded to, and the rabbi's act (making him forfeit the feast) is a change, not just a statement. That keeps it borderline rather than not.

07.event: Rav Hamnuna challenged Rava, and Rava was silent
07.turn: After Rav Hamnuna left, Rava rebuked himself for not answering and reasoned it out
07.outcome: He concluded that the answer he had missed was valid
07.summary: Rava could not answer Rav Hamnuna's challenge and was silent. After Rav Hamnuna left, Rava asked himself why he had not answered, doubted the answer, and then confirmed it from a baraita.
07.missing: Any action beyond silence, a departure and internal reasoning
07.reason: The passage is mainly speech and thought, with a small event (silence, the challenger leaving) and some tension and change. Between borderline and not, choose borderline.

08.actor: Residents of an alleyway; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
08.event: A case about an alleyway bounded by the sea and a garbage dump came before Rabbi
08.turn: Rabbi said neither prohibited nor permitted
08.summary: A question about an alleyway closed off by the sea on one side and a garbage dump on the other came before Rabbi. He said neither that it was prohibited nor that it was permitted, and the Gemara explains why.
08.missing: Any narrated action besides the case coming before the rabbi
08.reason: Coming before the rabbi is the only event, and he does not even rule. The rest is the Gemara's commentary.

09.event: He saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged by a pig
09.turn: He exclaimed, 'Shall a mouth that produced pearls lick dirt?'
09.summary: Aher saw the tongue of the martyred Hutzpit dragged along by a pig. Shocked, he cried out that a mouth that had produced pearls should lick dirt, and he went out and sinned.
09.reason: A post-biblical sage sees an event, reacts, and his life changes (he becomes a sinner). Several actions are connected by cause and lead to a change.

10.event: Rav Ami permitted first intercourse on Shabbat
10.turn: The Sages objected that the marriage contract was not written
10.outcome: He told them to have her seize movable property
10.summary: Rav Ami allowed a man to consummate his marriage on Shabbat. The Sages objected that her marriage contract had not been written, and he answered that she should take movable property as security.
10.missing: Any action beyond the ruling and the exchange
10.reason: It is mostly speech acts, but there is conflict and some implied change. This matches the editor's borderline verdict on Ketubot 7a:1.

11.event: A fox nested inside a turnip
11.summary: A fox once made its nest inside a turnip. When people weighed the turnip, it came to sixty litra by the measure of Tzippori.
11.missing: Causality and change. It is a single wonder cited as evidence
11.reason: There are events (the nesting, the weighing) but weak causality and no change, cited to support a teaching. This is shape 3 of R-C7, and close to the open one-line wonder case.

12.missing: Any event beyond seeing a place, which is cited as a measurement
12.reason: An eyewitness report of a place's size is cited as evidence in a legal objection. Nothing happens and nothing follows.

13.missing: Any event. A sage laughing at a teaching is a reaction inside scholarly discourse
13.reason: The passage is a teaching and a sage's dismissive reaction to it. That is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no event or change.

14.actor: Rav Nahman; Rav Adda bar Ahava; Rav Hana
14.event: Rav Nahman found them posing challenges to each other in the Pumbedita marketplace
14.outcome: He told them the case was still uncertain
14.summary: Rav Nahman came upon Rav Adda bar Ahava and his son-in-law Rav Hana debating a mishna in the Pumbedita market. He heard their distinction and told them that even in their case the law remained uncertain.
14.missing: Any event beyond the setting and the discussion
14.reason: A setting followed by a legal discussion is not enough (Shabbat 147a, Yevamot 17a). It is ordinary scholarly disagreement.

15.missing: Any event beyond the setting (leaning on a door bar) and an unresolved legal question
15.reason: A setting that only frames a legal dilemma is not a story.

16.actor: Rav Yosef; two holders of deeds
16.event: Two deeds for the same field came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one dated only Nisan
16.turn: He awarded the field to the dated deed, and the other claimant protested
16.outcome: The loser asked for an authorization to repossess, and Rav Yosef answered him
16.summary: Two buyers of the same field came before Rav Yosef with deeds dated the fifth of Nisan and only 'Nisan'. He gave the field to the dated deed. The other man protested, then asked for a document to recover his loss from later buyers, and Rav Yosef answered him.
16.missing: The end of the exchange runs into the next segment
16.reason: A case before a rabbi whose ruling awards the property, followed by a protest. It is mainly dialogue with some conflict, so borderline.

17.missing: Any turn or consequence. Two sages' practice is reported as evidence of how many blessings to recite
17.reason: A bare report of what Levi and Rav Asi did, cited as practice, with no response and nothing following.

18.missing: Any narrated event. Rabba bar Avuh's conditional statement is cited in a legal discussion, and no outcome is told
18.reason: It is a single statement of a condition, used to test a legal opinion. There is no event, no conflict and no outcome.

19.actor: An unnamed man; Rabbi Meir; the Sages
19.event: A man fell into the Great Cistern and came out after three days
19.turn: The Sages objected that miracles are not cited as precedent
19.outcome: The Gemara discusses what was miraculous about it
19.summary: Rabbi Meir cited the case of a man who fell into the Great Cistern and came out alive after three days. The Sages answered that miracles are not cited for law, and the Gemara asks what the miracle was.
19.missing: The incident is only alluded to; its details are in the mishna and are summarized by the translator
19.reason: A real incident with some change (falling in, surviving) is only alluded to here, quoted from the Mishnah, and then discussed. Borderline under R-C6.

20.actor: A man who betrothed a woman within three months and fled; Rafram
20.turn: Those involved asked Rafram what to do
20.outcome: Rafram ruled that his flight was penalty enough
20.summary: Rav Aha and Rafram disagreed about a man who betrothed a woman within three months and then fled. When such a case actually happened, Rafram ruled that the flight was penalty enough.
20.missing: The incident is only named; its content is the hypothetical case of the dispute
20.reason: An incident is only named and then ruled on, with nothing else narrated. Under R-C0's 2026-10-25 limit that is not a story.
